file_summaries.compressed_summary: CuTe DSL is a Python-based domain-specific language designed for dynamic compilation of high-performance GPU kernels. It bridges the gap between Python's user-friendliness and the performance demands of GPU programming by offering a high-level interface that maintains the power and control of CUDA. Key features include JIT compilation for both host and device code, seamless integration with major ML frameworks via DLPack, and intelligent caching to optimize repeated kernel executions. CuTe DSL is consistent with CuTe C++ abstractions, allowing users to leverage existing knowledge and patterns. It supports modern NVIDIA GPU architectures, including Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell, each offering advanced features like Tensor Cores and TMA. The DSL is particularly suited for custom GPU kernels in ML operations, high-performance numeric computation, and rapid prototyping of GPU algorithms. However, it is less ideal for simple operations or those already optimized in libraries like cuBLAS. CuTe DSL offers a medium learning curve for Python users, providing high control over GPU resources while avoiding the steep learning curve of raw CUDA. It is a powerful tool for Python developers and CUDA experts alike, enabling the development of efficient and optimized GPU kernels without the need to delve into CUDA C++.

file_summaries.title: CuTe DSL Decorators Overview
critical_patterns: Use @cute.jit to orchestrate GPU work from the CPU
Use @cute.kernel for writing GPU computation with explicit thread/block control
Common pattern: @cute.jit hosts function orchestrates @cute.kernel launch
Nesting @jit functions to launch multiple kernels for complex pipelines
constraints: Python functions cannot directly call @kernel functions
@kernel functions cannot call other @kernel functions
Control flow may not work with preprocessor=False
Must use .launch() to execute @kernel functions
file_summaries.compressed_summary: CuTe DSL provides two main decorators, @cute.jit and @cute.kernel, for generating optimized code through dynamic compilation. @cute.jit is used for host-side JIT-compiled functions that typically run on the CPU and manage GPU execution, while @cute.kernel is used for defining GPU kernel functions that require explicit grid and block configuration. The preprocessor parameter in both decorators controls the handling of loops and conditionals, with preprocessor=True automatically converting control flow to intermediate representation, which is recommended for most use cases. The no_cache parameter in @cute.jit controls JIT caching behavior, useful for debugging and testing. Kernel functions are launched using the .launch() method, specifying grid and block dimensions, and optionally, cluster dimensions, shared memory size, and CUDA stream. Python functions can call @jit functions directly but cannot call @kernel functions directly; instead, @jit functions can launch @kernel functions. A typical pattern involves using @cute.jit to orchestrate GPU work and @cute.kernel for the actual computation. Common pitfalls include forgetting to use .launch() for kernels, using @kernel for host code, and incorrect control flow handling with preprocessor=False. The documentation encourages using @cute.jit for orchestrating GPU work and preparing data, and @cute.kernel for parallel computation and explicit control over threads and blocks. Advanced usage includes nesting @jit functions to create complex pipelines. Related topics include quick start guides, code generation, and control flow handling.

file_summaries.compressed_summary: The CuTe DSL Quick Start Guide provides a foundational overview for developers looking to write GPU kernels using the CuTe DSL within the CUTLASS Python library. Key prerequisites include an NVIDIA GPU, CUDA 11.8+, and Python 3.8+. The guide walks through creating a simple vector addition kernel, emphasizing the use of thread and block indices for element-wise operations. It also covers more complex examples like matrix transposition using 2D indexing and element-wise operations with dynamic arguments, showcasing how to pass runtime parameters to kernels. The guide introduces compile-time constants for kernel specialization, allowing developers to optimize performance by eliminating unused code branches. Common patterns such as bounds checking, grid-stride loops, and multi-dimensional indexing are highlighted to ensure efficient and error-free kernel execution. Debugging tips include enabling logging, using cute.printf() for runtime debugging, and verifying results with PyTorch's assert_close(). Performance tips suggest choosing appropriate block sizes, minimizing divergence, coalescing memory access, and using shared memory for data reuse. The guide also outlines common errors and solutions, such as converting PyTorch tensors with from_dlpack() and ensuring valid grid/block configurations. Finally, it encourages further learning through topics like layouts, control flow, real-world examples, and optimization strategies.

Variables defined in control flow are not available outside
Cannot change variable types in control flow
No exceptions in dynamic control flow
Cannot mix compile-time and runtime values
Limited Python object support in kernels
No dynamic memory allocation in kernels
Limited type inference; explicit annotation may be needed
No automatic broadcasting like NumPy
Preprocessor=False has severe limitations
Architecture-specific requirements for tensor cores
Shared memory limits per block vary by architecture
Maximum threads per block and grid dimensions are architecture dependent
Limited Python debugging tools in kernels
JIT compilation overhead on first call
Dynamic shapes may be slower
Not supported in kernels: classes, OOP, generators, async/await, context managers, decorators, lambda functions, list/dict comprehensions
file_summaries.compressed_summary: CuTe DSL is designed with specific limitations to ensure safety, predictability, and performance. Understanding these constraints is crucial for writing effective GPU kernels. Dynamic control flow limitations include no early exits from loops and the isolation of variables defined within control blocks. Compile-time and runtime values must not be mixed, and dynamic memory allocation is not supported within kernels. The type system requires stability, with no automatic broadcasting of operations. Preprocessor mode, when set to False, introduces severe limitations such as branch collapse and loop unrolling. Architecture-specific constraints include shared memory limits and tensor core requirements. Threading and synchronization are subject to architecture-dependent limits on block and grid sizes. Debugging within kernels is limited, with standard Python tools being ineffective; instead, use cute.printf() and logging. Performance considerations include JIT compilation overhead and potential slowdowns with dynamic shapes. Language features such as classes, OOP, and async/await are not supported within kernels. Best practices involve starting simple, using default settings, validating early, profiling before optimization, and carefully reading error messages. When encountering limitations, consult documentation, simplify code, seek help, or consider alternative approaches like raw CUDA or Triton.
